style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 18 is a string of antithetic and observational proverbs clustered around two great themes: the tongue and human relationships. It opens with the man who cuts himself off from others (v.1) and closes with the friend who clings closer than a brother (v.24), framing the whole chapter between isolation and faithful bond. In between, the power of words runs like a current -- deep waters and a flowing brook (v.4), a fool's self-destroying mouth (vv.6-7), the gossip's morsels that sink deep (v.8), the verdict that life and death lie in the tongue's power (v.21). Woven through are warnings against pride before the fall (v.12), snap judgments before hearing (vv.13,17), and a single sure refuge: the name of the LORD, a strong tower for the righteous (v.10), set in deliberate contrast to the rich man's wall of wealth that stands only in his imagination (v.11).

1.text: The man who breaks away from others chases his own desire; against all sound wisdom he snarls and quarrels.
1.amp: The man who has separated [parad -- split off, divided himself from the company of others] himself seeks [baqash -- pursues] his own craving [taavah -- desire, longing, appetite]; against all sound wisdom [tushiyyah -- effective, success-bringing counsel] he breaks out in quarrel.
1.notes: parad (H6504) is to divide or split apart -- the same verb used in v.18 for the lot that parts strong men; here the self-isolator uses it on himself. taavah (H8378) is raw appetite. The loner of this proverb is not the contemplative but the contentious: cut off by choice, he treats every offered tushiyyah (H8454) as an enemy to be fought.

2.text: A fool takes no pleasure in understanding -- only in airing what is already in his own heart.
2.amp: A fool [kesil -- the thick-headed, the dullard] has no delight [chaphets -- takes no pleasure] in understanding [tebunah -- discernment], but only in laying bare [galah -- uncovering, exposing] his own heart [leb].
2.notes: kesil (H3684) is the obstinate fool of Proverbs, and galah (H1540) means to uncover or reveal -- elsewhere even 'to go into exile.' The fool has no appetite to take wisdom in; his single joy is to pour his own opinion out, exposing the empty room of his mind to all who will look.

3.text: When the wicked man arrives, contempt comes with him, and trailing close behind, disgrace brings reproach.
3.amp: When the wicked [rasha -- the guilty, the criminal] comes [bo -- enters, arrives], contempt [buz -- scorn, disdain] also comes [bo]; and with dishonor [qalon -- shame, ignominy] comes reproach [cherpah -- public reproach].
3.notes: rasha (H7563) is the guilty one, and the verse piles three shame-words -- buz (H937), qalon (H7036), cherpah (H2781) -- to show that wickedness never travels alone. Sin drags its own retinue of disgrace in after it; the entrance of the wicked is the entrance of contempt itself.

4.text: Deep as fathomless waters run the words a man speaks; yet wisdom's source breaks open like a brook that never stops flowing.
4.amp: The words [dabar -- speech, matters] of a man's [ish] mouth [peh] are deep [amoq] waters; the fountain [maqor -- source, spring] of wisdom [chokmah] is a flowing [naba -- bubbling up, pouring forth] brook [nachal -- stream, wadi].
4.notes: the proverb holds two images of speech in tension: deep waters (amoq, H6013) can be dark and hard to fathom, but maqor (H4726), a living spring, gushes fresh. naba (H5042) is to bubble up; chokmah (H2451) does not stagnate but flows -- the wise man's words are not a still cistern but a brook that keeps giving.

5.text: It is not good to show favor to the wicked, thrusting the righteous aside in judgment.
5.amp: It is not good [tov] to lift up the face [nasa panim -- to be partial to, to show favoritism toward] of the wicked [rasha], to thrust aside [natah -- to turn away, deflect] the righteous [tsaddiq] in judgment [mishpat].
5.notes: the idiom nasa panim (H5375 + H6440), literally 'to lift the face,' means to show partiality. natah (H5186), to turn or bend aside, here means to deny the righteous their due. To tilt the scales of mishpat (H4941) toward the guilty is not merely unwise but morally not-good -- a quiet understatement for a grave injustice God hates (cf. Deut 16:19).

6.text: A fool's lips march him into strife, and his mouth calls down a beating.
6.amp: A fool's [kesil] lips [saphah] enter [bo] into contention [riyb -- strife, legal dispute], and his mouth [peh] calls out [qara] for blows [makkah -- strokes, a beating].
6.notes: riyb (H7379) is a quarrel that can escalate to a lawsuit, and qara (H7121) is to summon or proclaim. The fool does not merely stumble into conflict -- his very lips issue the invitation, and his mouth all but shouts for the thrashing that answers it.

7.text: A fool's mouth is his undoing, and his lips are a snare laid for his own soul.
7.amp: A fool's [kesil] mouth [peh] is his ruin [mechittah -- destruction, downfall], and his lips [saphah] are a snare [moqesh -- a trap, a baited snare] to his soul [nephesh].
7.notes: moqesh (H4170) is a hunter's trap; the fool, by his careless speech, becomes both trapper and prey. Where verse 6 named the outward beating, verse 7 names the inward ruin -- his own words spring shut on his nephesh (H5315), his very life.

8.text: The words of a gossip are like choice morsels; they slide down into the inmost chambers of the body.
8.amp: The words [dabar] of a whisperer [nirgan -- a gossip, a slanderer] are like dainty morsels [delicacies eagerly swallowed]; they go down [yarad -- descend] into the innermost chambers [cheder -- inner rooms] of the belly [beten -- the inward parts].
8.notes: the gossip's words go down (yarad, H3381) like dainty food into the cheder (H2315), the secret inner rooms -- the same word for a bedchamber. Slander is relished, not resisted; it lodges deep in the beten (H990) and is not easily dislodged. The proverb repeats verbatim at 26:22, underscoring how memorable -- and how sweet to the flesh -- such poison is.

9.text: The man who is slack in his work is brother to the one who tears it all down.
9.amp: He who is slack [raphah -- lets his hands drop, grows lazy] in his work [melakah -- labor, occupation] is brother [ach -- kin] to the master [baal -- lord, owner] of destruction [shachath -- ruin, corruption].
9.notes: raphah (H7503) is to let the hands hang limp. The proverb's sting is in the kinship: the idler imagines himself harmless, but Solomon makes him brother (ach, H251) to the active destroyer (shachath, H7843). Neglect and vandalism arrive at the same ruined house from opposite roads.

10.text: The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous runs into it and is set on high, beyond reach.
10.amp: The name [shem -- name, reputation, revealed character] of the LORD [YHWH] is a strong [oz -- mighty, a stronghold] tower [migdal]; the righteous [tsaddiq] runs [ruts -- rushes] into it and is set on high [sagab -- lifted up out of danger, made unassailable].
10.notes: shem (H8034) is more than a label -- it is the LORD's revealed character, the whole of who He is. To it the tsaddiq (H6662) runs (ruts, H7323), and there he is sagab (H7682), set aloft beyond the enemy's reach. This is the chapter's hinge: against the rich man's wall in v.11, the only true fortress is the name of the LORD Himself.

11.text: The rich man's wealth is his fortified city, an unscalable wall -- but only in his own imagining.
11.amp: The rich man's [ashir] wealth [hon -- riches, substance] is his strong [oz] city [qiryah], and like a high [sagab -- lofty, unassailable] wall [chomah] in his own imagination [maskith -- a mental image, a fancy, even an idol-picture].
11.notes: the verse echoes v.10 word for word -- oz, sagab -- only to expose the counterfeit. The same strength the righteous finds in the LORD's name, the rich man imagines in his hon (H1952). But maskith (H4906) means a carved image or a picture in the mind; his fortress wall stands only where he has painted it, in his own conceit (cf. v.12's haughty heart heading for the fall).

12.text: Before the breaking comes, a man's heart is lifted high; but humility walks ahead of honor.
12.amp: Before destruction [sheber -- a breaking, a fracture, a shattering] the heart [leb] of a man [ish] is haughty [gabah -- lifted high, exalted in pride], but before honor [kabod -- glory, weight] is humility [anavah -- lowliness, meekness].
12.notes: gabah (H1361), to be high, is the pride that goes before sheber (H7667), the smash. The proverb sets two ascents against each other: the heart that climbs in pride is on its way down, while the way up to kabod (H3519) -- weighty honor -- runs through anavah (H6038), the lowly ground. The order is fixed and cannot be reversed (cf. 15:33; 1 Pet 5:5-6).

13.text: To answer a matter before you have heard it out -- that is folly, and it brings you shame.
13.amp: He who returns a word [shub dabar -- answers, replies] before he hears [shama -- listens to the whole of it], it is folly [ivvelet -- foolishness] and shame [kelimmah -- humiliation, disgrace] to him.
13.notes: shama (H8085) is to hear with attention, even to obey; the snap reply cuts the listening short. ivvelet (H200) is moral folly, not mere ignorance, and kelimmah (H3639) is the public humiliation it earns. The proverb rebukes the interrupter who has already decided before the speaker has finished (cf. Jas 1:19).

14.text: A man's spirit can carry him through sickness; but a spirit crushed -- who can lift that?
14.amp: The spirit [ruach -- breath, inner vitality] of a man [ish] will sustain [kul -- hold up, contain, bear] him in his sickness [machaleh -- illness, infirmity]; but a crushed [nakeh -- stricken, broken, contrite] spirit [ruach], who can bear [nasa -- lift, carry] it?
14.notes: ruach (H7307) is the inner life-breath that bears (kul, H3557) a man up under bodily illness. But when the ruach itself is nakeh (H5218) -- struck and broken -- the very thing that should do the lifting is shattered. The proverb measures inner wounds as graver than outer ones, and leaves its closing question open: who indeed can lift a broken spirit, but the One who heals it (cf. Ps 34:18; 51:17)?

15.text: The discerning heart acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise goes searching for it.
15.amp: The heart [leb] of the prudent [biyn -- the discerning, who tell things apart] gains [qanah -- acquires, gets as a possession] knowledge [daat], and the ear [ozen] of the wise [chakam] seeks [baqash -- searches after] knowledge [daat].
15.notes: qanah (H7069) is to acquire, even to buy -- knowledge is gotten as treasure, not stumbled upon. The verse pairs the inner organ and the outer: the discerning leb (H3820) takes daat (H1847) in, and the wise ozen (H241) actively hunts it down. Wisdom is never passive; even the already-wise keep seeking (cf. 1:5).

16.text: A man's gift opens the way before him and ushers him into the presence of the great.
16.amp: A man's [adam] gift [mattan -- a present freely given] makes room [rachab -- widens a way, opens space] for him, and leads [nachah -- guides, conducts] him before [panim -- into the presence of] great men [gadol].
16.notes: mattan (H4976) is simply a gift, and rachab (H7337) is to make broad -- the present clears a path through a crowded gate. The proverb is observational, not approving: it states a fact of how the world works, that a gift gains an audience with the gadol (H1419). Read alongside the warnings against bribes (v.5; 17:23), it describes a tool that may serve courtesy or corruption depending on the heart that gives.

17.text: The first to plead his case seems right -- until his neighbor comes and cross-examines him.
17.amp: He who is first [rishon] in his own cause [riyb -- legal dispute, lawsuit] seems just [tsaddiq -- in the right]; but his neighbor [rea -- the other party] comes [bo] and searches him out [chaqar -- examines, probes, cross-questions].
17.notes: rishon (H7223) is the first to speak; in a dispute (riyb, H7379) his account always sounds tsaddiq (H6662) until tested. chaqar (H2713) is to investigate thoroughly, to probe to the bottom. The proverb is a charter for fair hearing: no story is complete until the other side (rea, H7453) has had its cross-examination (cf. v.13's warning against answering before hearing).

18.text: Casting the lot puts an end to quarrels and separates contenders too strong to be parted otherwise.
18.amp: The lot [goral -- the cast lot, the assigned portion] causes contentions [madon -- strife, disputes] to cease [shabat -- to rest, to stop], and parts [parad -- separates, divides] between the mighty [atsum -- strong, powerful contenders].
18.notes: goral (H1486) is the sacred lot, understood to fall under the LORD's hand (16:33); when human argument cannot resolve a deadlock, the lot makes it shabat (H7673) -- cease, rest. parad (H6504) returns from v.1, but redeemed: there a man divided himself in pride, here the lot divides combatants in peace, keeping the atsum (H6099), the strong, from coming to blows.

19.text: A brother wronged is harder to win back than a fortified city, and such quarrels are like the iron bars of a citadel.
19.amp: A brother [ach] offended [pasha -- rebelled against, wronged, sinned against] is harder to win than a strong [oz] city [qiryah]; and their disputes [madon -- contentions] are like the bars [beriach -- bolts] of a citadel [armon -- fortress, palace].
19.notes: pasha (H6586) is to rebel or transgress -- the breach between kin runs deep. The strength-words gather: a wronged ach (H251) is more impregnable than a walled qiryah, and the estrangement bolts shut like the beriach (H1280) of an armon (H759). The closer the bond, the more bitter its breaking and the heavier its gates -- which is why v.24's friend who sticks closer than a brother shines so bright against this dark wall.

20.text: From the fruit of his mouth a man's belly is filled; with the harvest of his lips he is satisfied.
20.amp: A man's [ish] belly [beten -- the inward being] shall be satisfied [saba -- filled, sated] with the fruit [peri] of his mouth [peh]; with the increase [tebuah -- the harvest, the produce] of his lips [saphah] shall he be filled [saba].
20.notes: saba (H7646), to be sated, frames the verse like a meal. Speech is sown and reaped: peri (H6529), fruit, and tebuah (H8393), harvest, make a man's words a crop he must later eat. The proverb sets up v.21 -- what fills the beten (H990) may be nourishment or poison, depending on what was spoken.

21.text: Whether a man lives or dies lies within the tongue's grip; and whoever cherishes its use will feed on the harvest it yields.
21.amp: Death [mavet] and life [chay -- life, the living] are in the power [yad -- literally the 'hand,' the control] of the tongue [lashon -- tongue, speech]; and those who love [ahab] it shall eat [akal -- consume] its fruit [peri].
21.notes: yad (H3027), the hand, is the idiom for power and control -- the tongue (lashon, H3956) holds death and life in its grip. The harvest image of v.20 sharpens to a verdict: speech is never neutral. Those who love to wield the tongue will akal (H398) the very crop they grow with it, whether the bread of life or the bitter fruit of death (cf. Matt 12:36-37; Jas 3:5-10).

22.text: Whoever finds a wife finds something good, and draws favor from the LORD.
22.amp: Whoever finds [matsa -- discovers, attains] a wife [ishshah] finds [matsa] a good thing [tov], and obtains [puq -- draws out, brings forth] favor [ratson -- favor, delight, good pleasure] from the LORD [YHWH].
22.notes: matsa (H4672), to find, frames a wife as a discovery that is tov (H2896) -- good, the divine verdict over creation. ratson (H7522) is the LORD's favorable delight, and puq (H6329) means to obtain or draw out; the good marriage is not luck but grace, a token of God's smile. The whole gift descends from YHWH, not from the man's cleverness (cf. 19:14).

23.text: The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers him harshly.
23.amp: The poor [rush -- the destitute, the impoverished] speak [dabar] entreaties [tachanun -- supplications, pleas for grace]; but the rich [ashir] answer [anah -- respond, reply] roughly [az -- harshly, with fierce hardness].
23.notes: rush (H7326) is to be utterly poor; his only currency is tachanun (H8469), pleas for grace. The contrast is bitter: the rich (ashir, H6223) answer az (H5794) -- hard, fierce, strong-tongued. The proverb does not bless this hardness but exposes it, holding up a mirror to how wealth coarsens speech (cf. Jas 2:6) and quietly commending the gentler way.

24.text: A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who clings closer than a brother.
24.amp: A man [ish] of friends [rea -- companions, associates] may come to ruin [the shallow crowd that scatters in trouble], but there is [yesh -- there exists] one who loves [ahab -- a true friend, bound by love] who sticks closer [dabaq -- clings, cleaves fast] than a brother [ach].
24.notes: the verse turns on dabaq (H1695), to cling and cleave -- the same root used in Gen 2:24 for a man cleaving to his wife. Against the wide, brittle crowd of mere rea (H7453), there stands the one ohav (from ahab, H157) who holds fast even past the bond of an ach (H251). Christian readers have long heard in this closer-than-a-brother Friend a foreshadowing of Christ, who is not ashamed to call us brothers (Heb 2:11) and lays down His life for His friends (John 15:13).
